questions.prompt: Use the \(2\times 2\) formula to find the inverse of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: For \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), the inverse is (1/(ad - bc))\(\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\) if ad - bc is non-zero. Here ad - \(bc=1\)*4 - \(2\cdot3\) = -2. Therefore the inverse is (-1/2)\(\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Use the \(2\times 2\) formula to decide whether \(\begin{pmatrix}2&6\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\) has an inverse.
questions.answer: Compute ad - \(bc=2\)*3 - \(6\cdot1\) = 6 - 6 = 0. The determinant-like denominator in the inverse formula is zero, so the inverse formula is not defined. Therefore the matrix has no inverse.

questions.prompt: Set up the augmented matrix used to find the inverse of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\) by row reduction.
questions.answer: To compute an inverse by row reduction, augment A with the identity matrix of the same size. Since A is \(2\times 2\), use \(I_2\). The augmented matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\3&4&0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Row reducing the left block to \(I_2\) will turn the right block into \(A^{-1}\).

questions.prompt: Complete the inverse computation: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\0&-2&-3&1\end{pmatrix}\) is obtained while reducing [A | I]. Continue to find \(A^{-1}\).
questions.answer: Scale \(\mathbb R^2\) by -1/2 to get \((0,1,3/2,-1/2)\). Now eliminate the 2 above the pivot using \(\mathbb R^1\) <- \(\mathbb R^1\) - 2R2. This gives \(\mathbb R^1\) = [1, 0, 1 - 3, 0 - (-1)] = \((1,0,-2,1)\). The final matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-2&1\\0&1&3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore \(A^{-1}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Verify that \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is its own inverse.
questions.answer: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Compute \(A^2\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). The top-left entry is 1, top-right is 0, bottom-left is 0, and bottom-right is 1. Thus \(A^2\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Since \(AA=I\), \(A^{-1}\) = A.

questions.prompt: Find all real t such that \(\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\) has an inverse.
questions.answer: The matrix has an inverse when ad - bc is non-zero. Here ad - \(bc=t\)*1 - \(1\cdot2\) = t - 2. This is non-zero exactly when t != 2. Therefore the matrix is invertible for all real t except \(t=2\).

Multiply \(A^{-1}\) by b: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\)\(\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot 3 + (-2)\cdot 5\\0\cdot 3 + 1\cdot 5\end{pmatrix}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}-7\\5\end{pmatrix}\). Therefore x = \(\begin{pmatrix}-7\\5\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: A row reduction of [A | I] produces \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2&-1\\0&0&3&4\end{pmatrix}\). Explain why A has no inverse.
questions.answer: To find \(A^{-1}\) by row reduction, the left block must reduce to the identity matrix. Here the left block is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), which has a zero row and is not \(I_2\). This means A cannot be row reduced to the identity. Therefore A is not invertible and has no inverse.

questions.prompt: A learner tries to find the inverse of a \(2\times 3\) matrix by augmenting it with \(I_2\). Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Only square matrices can have two-sided inverses. A \(2\times 3\) matrix is not square, so it cannot have an inverse in the usual sense. The row-reduction method [A | I] for computing \(A^{-1}\) requires A to be n by n and uses \(I_n\). Therefore augmenting a \(2\times 3\) matrix with \(I_2\) is not a valid inverse computation.
